name: TV DIABLO Windows
note: v2187: He asked me to build the OCR liveness canary that would make the auto prune worth arming. I built it, and building it proved two things he needs before he decides anything. First, the rule is inverted with respect to risk. The prune deletes on a measured no, and no means OCR returned LINES and no stash panel was found, which is exactly what a tooltip covering the tab strip produces. On a stash screen the tooltip is the only place an item name appears, because a grid prints no names at all. So the single verdict this deletes on is the frame most likely to hold the last copy of a name, while the provably blank frames are the ones it keeps. Measured on his thirty reels with a 140 frame random sample and a full reel in mtime order, corroborated by the console own authority within one point: about five percent measured no, seven percent panel, and eighty eight percent SILENT, meaning the crop was made and OCR returned zero lines. The disk is in that eighty eight percent and a blank frame cannot carry a name. Second, freeing the blank frames needs proof the OCR lane was alive at that moment, otherwise no text on this frame and the reader was busy are the same observation, and the canary I built for that does not hold up. A cross family review returned six findings, four critical, and the one that blocks it is architectural rather than a bug: the blind counters are process globals and the console runs sweeps on other threads that move them, so a sweep ticking the silent counter inside the gate own delta collapses a tooltip frame into the deletable class. Per read counters are the prerequisite. Three of my own successive fixes to the canary broke each other, including one where consecutive silent frames vetoed one another so nothing could ever qualify, and silent frames come in runs of fifty nine on his reels. The attempt is deliberately kept out of the tree rather than half landed. This ship is comment only: the whole finding now sits at the arming switch so nobody flips it without reading what it costs.
